about: Justification trainer prompts for Unit 8 (docs/apphys-architecture.md, "Justification trainer").

prompts.title: Floating higher in salt water
prompts.context: A wooden block floats at rest in fresh water. It is moved to salt water, which is denser, and floats at rest again.
prompts.prompt: Predict whether more or less of the block is under the surface in salt water, and justify your prediction.
checklist: Claims less of the block is under water in salt water
Says floating at rest means the buoyant force balances the block's weight, so the buoyant force is the same in both liquids
Uses F_b = ρ_fluid V_under g: the same F_b with a larger ρ_fluid needs a smaller submerged volume

earns.answer: Less of the block is under water in salt water. The block floats at rest in both, so the buoyant force balances its weight each time; its weight has not changed, so the buoyant force is the same in both liquids. The buoyant force is F_b = ρ_fluid V_under g. Salt water has a larger density, so the same buoyant force needs a smaller submerged volume V_under, and the block floats higher.
earns.why: It uses the equilibrium of two separate forces and reads the dependence on the fluid's density correctly.

misses.answer: The salt water is denser, so it pushes up harder on the block and the buoyant force is bigger.
misses.why: The buoyant force cannot be bigger: the block floats at rest in both, so it equals the block's weight each time. The readers report this "denser fluid pushes harder" reasoning.

prompts.title: How fast a stone sinks at first
prompts.context: A granite stone (density 2700 kg/m³) is released from rest under water (density 1000 kg/m³). Ignore the water's drag at this low speed. Use g = 9.8 m/s².
prompts.prompt: Derive an expression for the stone's acceleration, calculate it, and explain why it is less than g.
checklist: Names two forces: the gravitational force of Earth down, ρ_stone V g, and the buoyant force of the water up, ρ_water V g
Uses Newton's second law: ρ_stone V a = ρ_stone V g − ρ_water V g, so a = g(1 − ρ_water/ρ_stone)
Calculates a = (9.8 m/s²)(1 − 1000/2700) = 6.2 m/s², less than g because the buoyant force points up and partly balances the weight

earns.answer: Two forces act on the stone: the gravitational force of Earth, down, of size ρ_stone V g, and the buoyant force of the water, up, of size ρ_water V g, where V is the stone's volume. By Newton's second law, (ρ_stone V)a = ρ_stone V g − ρ_water V g, so a = g(1 − ρ_water/ρ_stone) = (9.8 m/s²)(1 − 1000/2700) = 6.2 m/s², downward. It is less than g because the buoyant force points up, opposite the gravitational force, and cancels part of it.
earns.why: It keeps gravity and buoyancy as two separate forces in opposite directions, starts from Newton's second law, and shows the result.

misses.answer: Only the buoyant force acts under water, pushing up, so a = F_b/m = (1000/2700)(9.8) = 3.6 m/s² up.
misses.why: This drops the gravitational force, the error the readers report most on buoyancy questions. Both forces act on the stone, in opposite directions.

prompts.title: Reading a pressure-depth graph
prompts.context: A diver's gauge records the absolute pressure at several depths in a lake. The graph of pressure against depth is a straight line that crosses the pressure axis at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and has a slope of 1.0 × 10⁴ Pa/m. Use g = 9.8 m/s².
prompts.prompt: Explain what the intercept and the slope represent, and determine the density of the lake water.
checklist: Uses P = P₀ + ρgh, so the graph of P against depth h is a straight line
Says the intercept is P₀, the atmospheric pressure at the surface, and the slope is ρg
Finds ρ = slope/g = (1.0 × 10⁴ Pa/m)/(9.8 m/s²) = 1.0 × 10³ kg/m³, with the unit

earns.answer: The absolute pressure at depth h is P = P₀ + ρgh. So a graph of P against h is a straight line whose intercept, at h = 0, is P₀: the atmospheric pressure pushing on the lake surface, 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Its slope is ρg. So ρ = slope/g = (1.0 × 10⁴ Pa/m) / (9.8 m/s²) = 1.0 × 10³ kg/m³ (about 1020 kg/m³).
earns.why: It reads both features of the graph from the equation, including why the line does not start at zero, and finds ρ with its unit.

misses.answer: Pressure is proportional to depth, so at 10 m, ρ = P/(gh) = (2.0 × 10⁵)/(9.8 × 10) = 2.0 × 10³ kg/m³.
misses.why: Absolute pressure is not proportional to depth: the line has an intercept, the atmosphere's pressure. Ignoring it doubles the density here. The slope, not one point, gives ρg.

prompts.title: A hole four times as deep
prompts.context: Water leaks from a small hole in the side of a wide open tank, a depth h below the water surface. A second tank has a hole at depth 4h. Water is an ideal fluid.
prompts.prompt: Derive an expression for the speed of the water leaving a hole, and use it to compare the two jet speeds.
checklist: Applies Bernoulli's equation from the water surface to the hole: both are open to the air, so the pressures are equal (atmospheric)
Uses continuity to take the surface speed as about zero, because the tank is much wider than the hole
Gets ρgh = ½ρv², so v = √(2gh): the density cancels, and v ∝ √h, so the 4h hole gives twice the speed

earns.answer: Apply Bernoulli's equation along the flow from the water surface to the hole: P₁ + ρgy₁ + ½ρv₁² = P₂ + ρgy₂ + ½ρv₂². Both points are open to the air, so P₁ = P₂. The tank is much wider than the hole, so by continuity (A₁v₁ = A₂v₂) the surface moves very slowly: v₁ ≈ 0. That leaves ρgh = ½ρv², so v = √(2gh). The density cancels, and v is proportional to √h, so the hole at depth 4h gives a jet √4 = 2 times as fast.
earns.why: It starts from a named principle, states each simplification with its reason, and reads the square-root dependence correctly.

misses.answer: Four times the depth gives four times the pressure, so the water comes out four times as fast.
misses.why: Pressure at the hole does grow 4 times, but it sets the jet's kinetic energy per volume, ½ρv², not its speed. The speed grows as √h, so it doubles.
